scripts.objectives: Students will learn to tell living things from non-living things. They will also understand that non-living things do not grow, eat, or reproduce.
facts: The Merlion is a famous statue, but it is a non-living thing.
Non-living things do not need food, water, or air to survive.
You can spot the Merlion at Marina Bay spouting water, but it never grows bigger!

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that geckos are reptiles. They will also understand a key feature that makes reptiles different from other animals.
facts: A gecko is a reptile that has dry, scaly skin.
Geckos have sticky toe pads that help them climb walls and ceilings.
Many homes in Singapore have geckos that come out at night to catch insects near lights.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that fungi are a separate group from plants. They will also understand that fungi do not make their own food like plants.
facts: A mushroom is a fungus, not a plant or an animal.
Fungi do not have green leaves and cannot make food from sunlight.
You can find mushrooms growing on damp soil or logs after the rain in Singapore.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that living things respond to their surroundings. They will also understand how snails protect themselves.
facts: A snail is a living thing that carries its shell as a home.
When it senses danger, it pulls its soft body into the shell to stay safe.
You may spot snails crawling on leaves in HDB gardens after a rainy day.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that frogs are amphibians. They will also understand that amphibians can live both in water and on land.
facts: A frog is an amphibian that can live in water and on land.
Baby frogs called tadpoles live in water before they grow legs.
You can hear frogs croaking near ponds at Singapore parks after it rains.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that ferns are non-flowering plants. They will also understand that not all plants grow flowers.
facts: A fern is a non-flowering plant with feathery leaves called fronds.
Ferns make new plants using tiny spores instead of seeds or flowers.
You can see ferns growing on tree trunks and walls in shady Singapore parks.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that otters are mammals. They will also understand key features of mammals like fur and feeding on milk.
facts: Otters are mammals that breathe air and have fur on their bodies.
Baby otters drink milk from their mothers when they are young.
You can spot otter families swimming along Singapore's Kallang River and Marina Bay.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that mynahs are birds. They will also understand features birds share, like feathers and beaks.
facts: Mynahs are birds covered in feathers, with a beak and two legs.
Birds lay eggs, and many of them can fly to find food.
Mynahs hop around Singapore hawker centres looking for crumbs.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that butterflies are insects. They will also understand that insects have six legs and grow by changing form.
facts: Butterflies are insects with six legs and two pairs of wings.
They begin life as caterpillars before changing into butterflies.
You can watch many butterflies at the Changi Airport Butterfly Garden.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that a coconut is a giant seed. They will also understand how seeds travel to grow in new places.
facts: A coconut is a giant seed that can grow into a new palm tree.
Its light, floaty husk lets it travel across the sea to new lands.
Coconut palms grow along Singapore's beaches like Sentosa and East Coast.

scripts.objectives: Students will learn that sunflowers are flowering plants. They will also understand that plants need sunlight to grow.
facts: A sunflower is a flowering plant that turns to face the bright sun.
Its seeds can be eaten or planted to grow brand new sunflowers.
You can grow your own sunflowers in pots at home or in HDB community gardens.
